memory_candidates.content: Splitting a long-running test suite into a fast gating variant and a slow exhaustive variant without weakening assertions has a reliable four-part shape: (1) put instrumentation (progress callback, flushed JSONL side-channel, result artifact, completion marker) inside the ONE shared scan function as default-off parameters, so existing call sites are untouched and no second loop can drift; (2) persist a baseline manifest recording the known-decidable subset by BOTH index and canonical content, never index alone, so an enumerator/generator change fails loudly instead of silently misaligning; (3) have the gating variant assert the real soundness property over the decidable subset while asserting the undecidable set has not grown as a cheap structural invariant (population size fixed + membership fixed), rather than re-solving known-timeout items; (4) leave the exhaustive variant as the sole re-deriver of the full population and sole detector of drift. Two ordering constraints are load-bearing: the baseline must be derived BEFORE any gating assertion depends on it, from a contention-free serial run (a baseline derived under load permanently shrinks gating coverage -- the exact assertion-weakening the split exists to avoid), and the completion marker must be written strictly AFTER the result artifact is closed, since a marker that can precede a durable artifact reintroduces the false-completion failure mode.

When verifying a shared multi-tenant dev machine is 'idle' before a timing-sensitive test run, checking for competing pytest/xdist processes is not sufficient -- unrelated heavy CPU consumers from OTHER tools (observed: a `lean --worker` Lean 4 proof-search process sustaining 300-1200% CPU) can push near-budget Z3 solves over their timeout just as effectively as sibling pytest workers would, even inside a nominally-serial (`xdist_serial`, no `-n`) pytest pass. Diagnose intermittent solve-budget floor misses by checking `ps aux --sort=-%cpu` / `/proc/loadavg` for ANY heavy process, not just pytest; and corroborate with pre-existing, untouched tests in the same run failing the same way, which rules out a regression in whatever you just changed.
